newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar fails to advance vs yen by late Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: Dollar fails to advance vs yen by late Tokyo.

text.p: The dollar failed to advance against the yen by late Tokyo on Thursday, with reluctance to push it to a fresh high inviting long liquidations.

Overnight falls in sterling against the mark also weakened the yen selling interest, although the dollar's bottom was firmly blocked by talk of buying by Japanese investors such as pension funds, dealers in Tokyo said.
"Many people here are vaguely expecting the dollar to rise against the yen further, but they are taking a breather after its gains (until Wednesday)," said a dealer at a European bank in Tokyo.

The dollar hit a 33-month high of 112.34 yen in New York and Tokyo on Wednesday. It rose as high as 112.30 yen in Tokyo on Thursday. Friday's release of trade data on both sides of the Pacific has made some dealers and U.S. securities houses more subdued, dealers said. Japan's September trade balance figures are due at 2350 GMT on Thursday (8.50 a.m. on Friday) and U.S. August data at 1230 GMT on Friday.
Some dealers were concerned that a larger-than-expected U.S. trade deficit would prompt further long dollar liquidations as that occured the previous month.
"If the deficit is beyond market expectations, that may drag the dollar down, with stop-loss sales seen triggered at around 111.50 yen," said chief dealer at a Japanese bank.

But the dollar is otherwise unlikely to lose ground drastically because of persistent dollar-buying interest from Japanese investors in connection with their foreign securities investments. Japanese importers, lagging behind in their dollar purchases, are also intent on buying dollars on dips.
In afternoon trade, a U.S. securities house sold dollars against the yen in a relatively large amount, but the dollar soon got short-covering on back of investor dollar buying.
Currency dealers in Tokyo were showing little interest in Japan's general election on Sunday.
"Whichever party wins the majority in the election, the currency market's focus is on economic steps to be taken by a new government," said a bank dealer.
If the new government comes up with a large supplementary budget, that would push Japanese market interest rates up and in turn push the dollar down against the yen, he added.
A chief dealer at a U.S. bank in Singapore said there was more interest in the EMS crosses, focusing closely on a meeting between the Italian prime minister and German chancellor.

He said mark/lira looked strong but was likely to face resistance at 1002. "Mark/lira will likely continue to trade higher. It really depends on the outcome of the meeting," he said. Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick voiced strong doubts on Wednesday about the ability of weaker European countries like Italy and Spain to fix serious economic problems in time to qualify for a single European currency in 1999.
The remarks bolstered the mark's rally against the lira.
